cards.statement: Rust automatically drops an owned `String` when its owner leaves its scope.
cards.explanation: The owner controls the String's cleanup. Leaving its scope releases the string's allocation.

cards.statement: `let b = a;` keeps a `String` in `a` usable after the assignment.
cards.explanation: Assigning a String by value moves it into the destination. The compiler rejects subsequent use of the moved source.
cards.misconception: A String assignment leaves both bindings usable.

cards.statement: When code assigns a new `String` to `s`, Rust frees the old buffer at the end of `s`'s scope.
cards.explanation: Replacing an existing String drops its previous value immediately. Its old allocation is released during the assignment.
cards.misconception: Replacing a String delays cleanup of its old buffer until scope exit.

source.title: What Is Ownership? - The Rust Programming Language

cards.statement: An array `[T; N]` implements `Copy` automatically when its element type `T` implements `Copy`.
cards.explanation: Copy elements make the entire array eligible for implicit copying, regardless of its length.

cards.statement: `let b = a;` implicitly copies `a` when it has type `&mut String`.
cards.explanation: Mutable references do not implement Copy. Assignment transfers the reference rather than duplicating exclusive access.
cards.misconception: Mutable references are implicitly copied like shared references.

cards.statement: A nonempty `String` keeps the text bytes of its growable buffer on the heap.
cards.explanation: The Book separates a String's stack-held metadata from the heap allocation that stores its text.

cards.statement: A user-defined type implements `Copy` together with its own `Drop` implementation.
cards.explanation: Rust rejects combining Copy with Drop on the same type. Implicit duplication would conflict with its destruction semantics.
cards.misconception: A custom destructor and implicit copying coexist on one type.

cards.statement: A type implementing `Copy` also implements `Clone`.
cards.explanation: Copy declares Clone as a supertrait, so a Copy implementation carries that additional trait obligation.

cards.statement: Deriving `Copy` for a struct accepts fields whose types implement `Clone` alone.
cards.explanation: A derived Copy implementation requires every field type to implement Copy. Clone by itself does not satisfy that requirement.
cards.misconception: Clone fields are sufficient for deriving Copy.

cards.statement: For a local `p` whose struct type lacks a `Drop` impl, `let x = p.a;` leaves the `String` field `p.b` usable.
cards.explanation: For a struct without Drop held in a local variable, Rust tracks each field separately, so moving out one field leaves the others usable, though not the whole struct.

source.title: Field access expressions - The Rust Reference

cards.statement: A shadowing `let` binding inherits the fixed type of the earlier binding with that name.
cards.explanation: Shadowing introduces a new binding, which can have a different type from the binding that previously used that name.
cards.misconception: Shadowing preserves a variable's type like reassignment does.

cards.statement: Passing `&s` to a function leaves ownership of the `String` with the caller.
cards.explanation: A function receiving &String borrows the caller's value. The caller continues to own that String.

cards.statement: A function receiving `&String` modifies that string with `push_str`.
cards.explanation: String::push_str needs mutable access. A shared &String parameter permits reading the string rather than changing its buffer.
cards.misconception: A shared String reference provides write access to its buffer.

cards.statement: Taking `&mut x` from an owned local `i32` binding requires declaring `x` as `mut`.
cards.explanation: An owned local needs a mutable binding before code can borrow that local mutably.

cards.statement: `let a = &mut s; let b = &mut s;` compiles when `a` is still used after `b` is created.
cards.explanation: The first mutable borrow of s stays live until a's last use, so creating b in the meantime is a second simultaneous &mut borrow, which the borrow checker rejects.
cards.misconception: A second mutable borrow of the same value is fine while the first one is still used later.

source.title: References and Borrowing - The Rust Programming Language

cards.statement: Rust accepts a mutable borrow after a shared reference's last use in the same block.
cards.explanation: The borrow checker recognizes when a reference stops being used. The later mutable borrow can begin before the block ends.

cards.statement: `let r = &mut x;` requires `mut r` to change the integer `x` through `r`.
cards.explanation: The binding r can stay immutable while *r changes x. A mutable reference grants access to its referent independently of rebinding r.
cards.misconception: Writing through a mutable reference needs a mutable reference binding.

cards.statement: Rust rejects returning a reference to a function-owned local `String`.
cards.explanation: The local String is destroyed as the function ends. The borrow checker rejects a return value that would refer to that expired local.

cards.statement: Rust accepts simultaneous mutable borrows of different fields in a local struct.
cards.explanation: The compiler treats directly accessed struct fields as separate places, so borrowing one field leaves another available.

cards.statement: Calling an `&self` method on an owned struct requires an explicit `&` on the receiver.
cards.explanation: Method-call syntax adds the reference needed for an &self receiver. An owned value can call that method with value.method().
cards.misconception: Method receivers need the same explicit borrowing syntax as ordinary function arguments.

cards.statement: Rust accepts `v.push(4)` while a reference to an element of `v` is used after the push.
cards.explanation: Vec::push may relocate the vector's allocation. The borrow checker rejects pushing while an element reference remains in use.
cards.misconception: A vector element reference stays valid across a push.

source.title: Storing Lists of Values with Vectors

cards.statement: Adding `'a` to a reference extends the lifetime of the value it refers to.
cards.explanation: Lifetime annotations describe relationships between references. They do not lengthen the lifetime of any referenced value.
cards.misconception: Lifetime annotations keep borrowed values alive for longer.

cards.statement: `fn choose(x: &str, y: &str) -> &str` needs an explicit output lifetime.
cards.explanation: The two input lifetimes make the output ambiguous. The signature needs to specify which lifetime the returned reference follows.

cards.statement: The Book's annotated `longest` result stays usable until the longer-lived input expires.
cards.explanation: The Book's longest signature ties both inputs and its result to one lifetime. The caller can use the result within the inputs' shared, shorter lifetime.
cards.misconception: The returned longest slice follows the longer-lived input.

cards.statement: `struct View { text: &str }` needs an explicit lifetime on its reference field.
cards.explanation: Rust requires a lifetime annotation on that reference field. A declared lifetime parameter can connect the field's borrow to the struct.

cards.statement: In `fn head(s: &str, n: usize) -> &str`, elision ties the returned reference to the lifetime of `s`.
cards.explanation: Only one lifetime appears among the parameters, since usize holds none, so elision assigns it to the elided output and the signature needs no annotation.

cards.statement: Elision in `fn pick(&self, other: &str) -> &str` ties the output lifetime to `self`.
cards.explanation: A reference receiver supplies elided output lifetimes, even when the method has other reference parameters.

cards.statement: Elision gives the result of `fn text() -> &str` a `'static` lifetime.
cards.explanation: With no input lifetime to select, output lifetime elision fails. The return reference needs an explicit lifetime.
cards.misconception: A reference return with no reference input defaults to static.

cards.statement: `Thing<'_>` asks Rust to infer a lifetime argument in a type path.
cards.explanation: The '_ placeholder requests lifetime inference. The Reference prefers it for lifetimes in type paths.

cards.statement: Since Rust 1.89, `mismatched_lifetime_syntaxes` rejects mixed lifetime syntax by default.
cards.explanation: The mismatched_lifetime_syntaxes lint warns by default about inconsistent lifetime syntax between inputs and outputs. It does not make that syntax an error by default.
cards.misconception: Mixed lifetime spelling becomes a hard compiler error by default.

cards.statement: The Rust Book says a `'static` suggestion in an error usually signals a dangling reference to fix.
cards.explanation: The Book advises checking whether the reference can actually live that long. Its guidance is to repair the underlying lifetime problem.

cards.statement: `T: 'a` guarantees that a value of type `T` remains allocated for the whole lifetime `'a`.
cards.explanation: T: 'a constrains the lifetimes contained in T to outlive 'a. It does not keep a particular value of T alive.
cards.misconception: An outlives bound controls the allocation lifetime of each value.

cards.statement: Rust gives string literals type `&'static str`, including literals inside functions.
cards.explanation: A string literal's text remains valid for the duration of the program. Using it in a local binding does not shorten that storage lifetime.

cards.statement: `String::len` returns the number of bytes stored in its UTF-8 text buffer.
cards.explanation: UTF-8 can use several bytes for one Unicode scalar value, so the byte count differs from a character count.

cards.statement: Indexing a `String` with `s[0]` yields its first character as a `char` value.
cards.explanation: String does not support indexing by a single integer. UTF-8's variable-width encoding prevents that syntax from selecting a character.
cards.misconception: Integer indexing extracts a character from a String.

source.title: Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings

cards.statement: Rust panics when code slices a `String` at a byte position inside a UTF-8 character.
cards.explanation: String ranges use byte positions. The endpoints need to fall on UTF-8 character boundaries to produce a valid string slice.

cards.statement: A `char` stores one user-perceived character, including a multi-scalar emoji.
cards.explanation: Rust's char represents one Unicode scalar value. A displayed character can consist of multiple scalar values.
cards.misconception: A Rust char represents a whole grapheme rather than one Unicode scalar value.

cards.statement: `left + right` borrows `left` when `left` is a `String` and `right` is an `&str`.
cards.explanation: String addition takes its left operand by value. That String moves into the addition operation.
cards.misconception: String addition borrows its left String operand.

source.title: Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings

cards.statement: `String::push` appends one `char` to the existing UTF-8 text buffer.
cards.explanation: The method encodes the supplied Unicode scalar value as UTF-8 and appends its bytes to the existing String.

cards.statement: `String::from_utf8` replaces malformed UTF-8 byte sequences with replacement characters.
cards.explanation: String::from_utf8 validates the byte vector and returns Err for invalid UTF-8. It preserves the String type's valid UTF-8 invariant.
cards.misconception: String::from_utf8 repairs invalid byte sequences rather than reporting an error.

cards.statement: For an array with enough elements, `&a[1..=3]` includes the element at index 3.
cards.explanation: The start..=end syntax builds a RangeInclusive, which contains its end value, so slicing with 1..=3 borrows the elements at indexes 1, 2 and 3.

cards.statement: `slice.get(i)` panics when `i` lies beyond the slice's last element.
cards.explanation: For an out-of-bounds index, slice::get returns None. Its Option result makes the missing element explicit.
cards.misconception: The get method handles invalid indices by panicking.

cards.statement: Rust treats `[i32; 3]` and `[i32; 4]` as different types despite matching element types.
cards.explanation: An array's element count is part of its type. Changing the length changes the array type even when its element type stays the same.

cards.statement: `struct Meters(u32); struct Seconds(u32);` gives the two names interchangeable argument types.
cards.explanation: Tuple structs create distinct types. Even with identical field types, a value of Meters does not satisfy a parameter whose type is Seconds.
cards.misconception: Matching field types make values of different tuple structs interchangeable.

cards.statement: For `struct Ready;`, `let ready = Ready;` constructs a value of type `Ready`.
cards.explanation: Rust reads Ready in expression position as a value of the unit-like struct. No constructor argument list is needed.

cards.statement: Field init shorthand initializes `name` from the struct type's default value for `name`.
cards.explanation: Field init shorthand uses the value bound to the same name in scope. Writing name is shorthand for name: name.
cards.misconception: Field init shorthand obtains values from type-level field defaults.

cards.statement: A named struct declaration uses `mut field: Type` to enable field reassignment.
cards.explanation: The mut modifier applies to the instance binding. A struct declaration does not assign separate mut modifiers to individual fields.
cards.misconception: A struct declaration assigns mutability separately to named fields.

cards.statement: Inside `impl Counter`, the receiver `&self` has type `&Counter`.
cards.explanation: &self abbreviates self: &Self. Inside impl Counter, Self denotes Counter, so the receiver's type is &Counter.

cards.statement: A second inherent `impl` block can replace a struct's previously defined methods.
cards.explanation: Inherent impl blocks for one type add their items together. Reusing a method name that an earlier impl block of the type already defines is a duplicate definition the compiler rejects.
cards.misconception: A later inherent impl block overwrites the type's previously defined methods.

cards.statement: An enum can combine unit variants, tuple variants and variants with named fields.
cards.explanation: Enum variants belong to one type while their fields may use different shapes. A single enum may include unit, tuple and struct variants.

cards.statement: Rust automatically makes a tuple enum variant's constructor usable as a function value.
cards.explanation: A tuple variant's constructor takes its fields as parameters and returns the enum type. It coerces to a function pointer with the matching signature.

cards.statement: Rust automatically unwraps `Some(3)` for the assignment `let n: i32 = Some(3);`.
cards.explanation: Option<i32> and i32 are distinct types. Rust rejects assigning Some(3) directly to an i32; the programmer handles the Option explicitly.
cards.misconception: Rust implicitly extracts a present value when an expression expects the inner type.

cards.statement: For `enum Mode { Fast, Slow }`, `Mode::Slow as u8` evaluates to the variant's integer discriminant.
cards.explanation: A unit-variant enum such as Mode with no Drop implementation supports integer casts. as u8 reads the selected variant's discriminant.

cards.statement: Rust checks a `match` on `Option<i32>` for coverage of both `Some(_)` and `None`.
cards.explanation: An Option match has to account for both variants. Rust rejects a match whose patterns leave a possible value uncovered.

cards.statement: A catch-all `_` pattern directly binds the matched value for use inside its match arm.
cards.explanation: The wildcard _ ignores the matched value instead of introducing a variable. A named catch-all pattern binds that value for the arm to use.
cards.misconception: The wildcard retains the matched value as an accessible binding.

source.title: All the Places Patterns Can Be Used

cards.statement: A guarded `_ if ready` arm counts as a catch-all when Rust checks `match` exhaustiveness.
cards.explanation: A guard can fail even when its arm's pattern matches. Rust therefore excludes guarded arms from the coverage that proves a match exhaustive.
cards.misconception: A wildcard remains exhaustive even when a Boolean guard limits its arm.

cards.statement: Matching an `Option<i32>` with `whole @ Some(1..=5)` binds the complete option to `whole`.
cards.explanation: An @ binding keeps the value matched by its subpattern. Here whole holds the entire Some value, rather than just its integer payload.

cards.statement: For local `struct Point { x: i32, y: i32, z: i32 }`, `Point { x, .. }` binds `x`.
cards.explanation: In a struct pattern, .. stands for the remaining fields. Point { x, .. } selects x while ignoring the other fields.

cards.statement: The else block in `let...else` supplies a fallback value for an unsuccessful binding.
cards.explanation: The else block of let...else has to diverge, such as by returning or panicking. It cannot finish normally and continue with an unsuccessful binding.
cards.misconception: A let...else failure block assigns a fallback value to the binding.

cards.statement: `fn take(Some(x): Option<i32>) {}` unwraps `Some` arguments in its parameter list.
cards.explanation: Rust rejects Some(x) as an Option parameter pattern because None can fail to match it. Function parameter patterns have to be irrefutable.
cards.misconception: Function parameters can use patterns that match just one enum variant.

source.title: Refutability: Whether a Pattern Might Fail to Match

cards.statement: A `while let Some(x) = values.pop()` loop exits when `pop` returns `None`.
cards.explanation: A while let loop stops when its condition's pattern fails. None fails to match Some(x), so execution continues after the loop.

cards.statement: Since Rust 1.95, an `if let` match guard exposes its pattern bindings in that arm's body.
cards.explanation: A successful conditional let guard brings its new variables into scope in the corresponding arm, alongside bindings from the arm's main pattern.

cards.statement: `Result::unwrap` returns an `Err` value to its caller when the result contains an error.
cards.explanation: Result::unwrap panics on Err. Its failure path stops ordinary execution instead of returning the error as a value.
cards.misconception: Unwrapping a failed Result returns the error for the caller to handle.

cards.statement: `Option::map` preserves `None` when mapping a missing value.
cards.explanation: Option::map transforms a present payload. A missing input stays None in the resulting Option.

cards.statement: `Result::and_then` wraps its closure's returned `Result` in an additional `Ok`.
cards.explanation: When and_then invokes its closure, the closure's Result becomes the method's result. The method adds no outer Ok layer.
cards.misconception: and_then wraps the callback's Result in another Result instead of returning it directly.

cards.statement: A call to `Result::unwrap_or_else` on `Ok(7)` skips evaluation of its fallback closure.
cards.explanation: unwrap_or_else receives a closure, so it computes a fallback on demand. A successful result supplies its stored value instead.

cards.statement: In a `Result`-returning function, `?` converts a propagated error through `From::from`.
cards.explanation: The error branch of Result-based ? returns Err(From::from(e)). The conversion targets the enclosing function's error type.

cards.statement: `?` converts an `Option<T>` into a `Result<T, E>` using the function's return type.
cards.explanation: In a function returning Result, ? does not convert Option into Result. An explicit conversion such as ok_or supplies the missing error.
cards.misconception: The question mark operator infers an error when converting Option to Result.

cards.statement: Rust accepts `Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>` as the return type of `main`.
cards.explanation: The Book uses this signature for a fallible main function. Returning Ok(()) reports success, while returning Err reports failure.

cards.statement: Rust warns by default when `save();` ignores `save`'s `Result<(), std::io::Error>` return value.
cards.explanation: Result carries a must-use annotation. The default warning draws attention to a fallible operation whose outcome the code ignores.

cards.statement: With `panic = "abort"`, Rust unwinds stack frames before terminating the process.
cards.explanation: The abort panic strategy terminates the process directly. It does not unwind the stack or run stack-local destructors.
cards.misconception: The abort panic strategy unwinds before exiting.

cards.statement: In a default release build, Rust panics when integer addition overflows at run time.
cards.explanation: Default release settings disable overflow checks. Runtime integer addition wraps in two's complement when the mathematical sum exceeds the type's range.
cards.misconception: Default release builds check runtime integer addition for overflow and panic.

cards.statement: `std::process::exit` runs destructors for local values before ending the process.
cards.explanation: process::exit ends the process immediately. It skips destructors for values on every thread's stack.
cards.misconception: Explicit process exit performs normal stack-local cleanup.

cards.statement: A trait's default method can call a required method from the same trait on the current receiver.
cards.explanation: A default trait method uses the implementation of the required method supplied by the implementing type.

cards.statement: A function returning `impl Display` can return a `String` or an `i32` on different branches.
cards.explanation: Return-position `impl Trait` represents one concrete type per function instantiation. Different branches returning `String` and `i32` violate that requirement.
cards.misconception: A shared trait implementation makes distinct concrete return types interchangeable under impl Trait.

cards.statement: Rust compiles a generic function into versions tailored to the concrete types used by its callers.
cards.explanation: During compilation, Rust substitutes the concrete types used by callers into generic code. This process is called monomorphization.

cards.statement: The orphan rule rejects a `Display` implementation for a local tuple struct holding `Vec<String>`.
cards.explanation: A newtype wrapper defined in your crate is a local type. Your crate can implement the foreign `Display` trait for that wrapper.
cards.misconception: Wrapping a foreign type leaves the wrapper foreign for the orphan rule.

cards.statement: One type can implement `Iterator` repeatedly by choosing a different `Item` per implementation.
cards.explanation: An `Iterator` implementation fixes one `Item` type for its implementing type. A second implementation with another `Item` conflicts with the first.
cards.misconception: An associated type behaves like a trait generic parameter that distinguishes separate implementations.

cards.statement: A plain generic type parameter `T` has an implicit `?Sized` bound by default.
cards.explanation: A plain generic type parameter has an implicit `Sized` bound. Writing `T: ?Sized` relaxes that bound so the parameter also admits unsized types.
cards.misconception: Generic type parameters admit unsized types through a default ?Sized bound.

cards.statement: Rust allows `dyn T` for the trait `trait T { fn f<U>(&self) where Self: Sized; }`.
cards.explanation: The method's `Self: Sized` bound excludes it from trait-object dispatch. Its type parameter therefore leaves this trait dyn compatible.

cards.statement: Since Rust 1.86, trait object upcasting changes `&dyn Super` into `&dyn Sub` when `Sub: Super`.
cards.explanation: Trait object upcasting follows the supertrait direction: `&dyn Sub` coerces to `&dyn Super` when `Sub: Super`.
cards.misconception: Trait object upcasting converts a supertrait object into an object of its more specific subtrait.

cards.statement: In the 2021 edition, writing a trait object type requires the `dyn` keyword before the trait name.
cards.explanation: Edition 2021 requires the explicit `dyn` spelling for trait object types, such as `&dyn Display`.

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, default return-position `impl Trait` capture limits lifetimes to those written in its bounds.
cards.explanation: Default return-position `impl Trait` capture in edition 2024 includes every in-scope generic parameter, including lifetime parameters.
cards.misconception: The 2024 default capture rules retain the earlier requirement to mention captured lifetimes in return-type bounds.

cards.statement: `#[derive(Display)]` automatically supplies `{}` formatting for a struct.
cards.explanation: Rust's built-in derive supports Debug for {:?}. Display formatting with {} needs an implementation written by the programmer.
cards.misconception: Rust derives Display just as it derives Debug.

source.title: Derivable Traits - The Rust Programming Language

cards.statement: A derived `Clone` implementation preserves sharing through an `Arc<Mutex<T>>` field.
cards.explanation: Derived Clone calls clone on the struct's fields. Cloning an Arc<Mutex<T>> field retains a handle to the existing allocation, so the protected state remains shared.

cards.statement: When their block ends, Rust drops its remaining local variables in declaration order.
cards.explanation: At the end of a scope, Rust drops remaining local variables in reverse declaration order. Later declarations are cleaned up before earlier ones.
cards.misconception: Rust cleans up local variables in the order they were declared.

cards.statement: `#[derive(Default)]` on an enum makes its first unit variant the default value.
cards.explanation: Derived Default needs a #[default] marker on a unit variant; declaration order does not select the value. Default::default() returns the marked variant.
cards.misconception: Deriving Default chooses the earliest unit variant automatically.

cards.statement: A value of type `f64` satisfies an `Eq` trait bound on a generic function parameter.
cards.explanation: f64 implements PartialEq rather than Eq. NaN compares unequal to itself, so floating-point equality lacks Eq's reflexivity guarantee.
cards.misconception: Floating-point equality satisfies the same Eq contract as integer equality.

cards.statement: Deriving `PartialOrd` on a struct gives earlier declared fields priority during comparison.
cards.explanation: Derived PartialOrd compares fields lexicographically from top to bottom. Later fields matter after preceding field comparisons return equal.

cards.statement: `impl From<Source> for Target` automatically enables `Source: Into<Target>`.
cards.explanation: The standard library's blanket implementation provides Into<Target> for Source when Target implements From<Source>. The conversion follows the same From implementation.

cards.statement: In the 2021 edition, `TryFrom` and `TryInto` are in scope through the standard prelude.
cards.explanation: Rust 2021's prelude imports TryFrom and TryInto for ordinary Rust code, making their trait methods available in scope.

source.title: Additions to the prelude - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: A `String` satisfies an `AsRef<Vec<u8>>` bound for code that reads its UTF-8 bytes.
cards.explanation: String implements AsRef<[u8]>, exposing its UTF-8 data as a borrowed byte slice. It does not implement AsRef<Vec<u8>>.
cards.misconception: String implements AsRef<Vec<u8>> to expose its byte storage.

cards.statement: Deref coercion converts an owned `Box<i32>` argument into the `i32` expected by a function.
cards.explanation: Rust applies Deref coercion to reference arguments. A function taking &i32 accepts &Box<i32>; an i32 parameter still expects a plain integer.
cards.misconception: Deref coercion extracts a smart pointer's owned value to satisfy a value parameter.

cards.statement: For an owned `String` named `text`, the closure `move || text.len()` implements `Fn`.
cards.explanation: The move keyword determines capture by value. This closure reads its captured String through a shared borrow, so its body satisfies Fn.

cards.statement: For an owned `String` named `text`, the closure `|| text` implements `FnMut`.
cards.explanation: Returning the captured String moves it out of the closure. The closure implements FnOnce, but its body prevents repeated calls through FnMut.
cards.misconception: A closure can implement FnMut while moving its captured String out on invocation.

cards.statement: `let f: fn(i32) -> i32 = |x| x + 1;` coerces the closure to a function pointer.
cards.explanation: This ordinary closure captures no environment values. Rust coerces it to a function pointer with the matching parameter and return types.

cards.statement: Inside `fn run<F: FnOnce()>(f: F)`, passing `f` to a parameter bounded by `Fn()` compiles.
cards.explanation: Fn has FnMut and FnOnce as supertraits, so every Fn type also satisfies FnOnce. A type known only to be FnOnce gives no Fn guarantee, so the call is rejected.
cards.misconception: A FnOnce bound is enough to satisfy an Fn bound because the closure traits form a supertrait chain.

cards.statement: In the 2021 edition, `|| pair.0.len()` captures both fields of a local `(String, String)` tuple.
cards.explanation: Edition 2021 permits closures to capture individual fields. This closure captures the first tuple field, leaving the second outside its capture.
cards.misconception: Accessing one field in a closure captures the entire tuple in edition 2021.

source.title: Disjoint capture in closures - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: `iter.map(f)` immediately runs `f` over the iterator's remaining items.
cards.explanation: Iterator::map creates an adapter and calls f as that adapter yields items. Creating the adapter alone leaves those transformations unevaluated.
cards.misconception: Creating a map iterator eagerly invokes its closure over the input.

cards.statement: A `Vec<_>` result annotation tells `collect()` which container type to build.
cards.explanation: Iterator::collect uses the expected result type to select a collection. Vec<_> supplies the container type while Rust infers the element type.

cards.statement: The iterator from `iter()` on a `Vec<String>` yields borrowed `&String` items.
cards.explanation: Vec::iter produces shared references to elements in the vector. The iterator gives access to the existing strings through borrowing.

source.title: Processing a Series of Items with Iterators

cards.statement: In the 2021 edition, `.into_iter()` on a `[String; 2]` yields owned `String` values.
cards.explanation: The array method call uses the array's by-value IntoIterator implementation in edition 2021. Its items are owned elements from the array.

source.title: IntoIterator for arrays - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, `b.into_iter()` borrows `b` when `b` has type `Box<[String]>`.
cards.explanation: In edition 2024, this method call consumes the boxed slice and returns an iterator over owned String values. The original box is moved.
cards.misconception: The boxed-slice into_iter method call keeps borrowing the box in edition 2024.

source.title: Add IntoIterator for Box<[T]> - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: `collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()` keeps requesting items after the iterator yields `Err`.
cards.explanation: Collecting into Result stops at the first Err and returns that error. It leaves subsequent iterator items unrequested.
cards.misconception: Collecting Result items continues past an Err before choosing the returned error.

cards.statement: `Box::new(42_i32)` places the integer payload on the heap behind the resulting `Box<i32>` pointer.
cards.explanation: Box::new allocates the i32 on the heap. The Box value holds a pointer to that allocation.

source.title: Using Box<T> to Point to Data on the Heap

cards.statement: For `enum List { Cons(i32, List), Nil }`, the compiler uses `Nil` to give `List` a finite size.
cards.explanation: A direct List field leaves the enum's layout recursively unbounded despite Nil. Replacing that field with Box<List> gives the recursive link a known size.
cards.misconception: A recursive enum's terminating variant also terminates compile-time layout recursion.

source.title: Using Box<T> to Point to Data on the Heap

cards.statement: A `Box<dyn std::fmt::Display>` value has a size known at compile time despite its unsized target.
cards.explanation: Pointers to trait objects have a fixed layout containing pointer information and metadata. The trait object they point to is dynamically sized.

source.title: Dynamically sized types - The Rust Reference

cards.statement: `Rc::clone(&value)` allocates a separate copy of the pointed-to `String` and its text buffer.
cards.explanation: Rc::clone creates another owner of the same allocation and increments its strong count. It leaves the pointed-to String and its text buffer shared.
cards.misconception: Cloning an Rc<String> duplicates the inner String rather than its ownership handle.

cards.statement: A mutable binding lets its owner change a shared `Rc<Vec<i32>>`'s elements through dereferencing.
cards.explanation: Rc dereferencing provides shared access even through a mut binding. Changing data shared by its owners needs interior mutability, such as an Rc<RefCell<Vec<i32>>>.
cards.misconception: Marking an Rc binding mut makes its shared pointee mutably accessible.

cards.statement: `std::rc::Weak::upgrade` returns an `Option<Rc<T>>` to account for the allocation's value expiring.
cards.explanation: Weak::upgrade returns Some(Rc<T>) when upgrading succeeds and None after the inner value has been dropped. A weak pointer leaves the value free to expire.

cards.statement: A strong `Rc<T>` reference cycle can leak its values while the program retains Rust's memory safety.
cards.explanation: Strong references around an Rc cycle keep its values allocated. Rust's memory safety guarantees permit memory leaks.

cards.statement: Calling `get` on a `Cell<i32>` can return a shared reference to the integer stored inside the cell.
cards.explanation: Cell<i32>::get returns an i32 copied from the cell's current value. Cell::get is available when the contained type implements Copy.
cards.misconception: Cell::get borrows its inner value and returns a shared reference.

cards.statement: The compiler resolves conflicts between `RefCell::borrow` and `RefCell::borrow_mut` during compilation.
cards.explanation: RefCell tracks its active borrows at run time. Its borrow and borrow_mut methods panic when the requested borrow conflicts with the active state.
cards.misconception: RefCell's borrow conflicts receive the same compile-time validation as ordinary references.

source.title: RefCell<T> and the Interior Mutability Pattern

cards.statement: `Cell<T>`, `RefCell<T>` and `OnceCell<T>` implement `Sync` when their contained type `T` implements `Sync`.
cards.explanation: Cell, RefCell and OnceCell do not implement Sync, even with a Sync inner type. Their shared mutation interfaces serve single-threaded access.
cards.misconception: A Sync inner type makes these cell containers Sync as well.

cards.statement: `Arc<T>` updates its reference counts with atomic operations, adding overhead compared with `Rc<T>`.
cards.explanation: Arc uses atomics to coordinate ownership counts across threads. Its documentation identifies their extra cost compared with ordinary memory accesses.

cards.statement: `std::thread::spawn` requires its closure to implement `Send` and satisfy `'static`.
cards.explanation: The Send bound checks that captured data is safe to transfer to the new thread. The 'static bound excludes closures borrowing shorter-lived data.

cards.statement: `JoinHandle::join` rethrows a joined thread's Rust panic in the calling thread.
cards.explanation: JoinHandle::join returns Err when the joined thread unwinds from a Rust panic. Calling code receives the panic payload as the error value.
cards.misconception: Joining a panicked thread automatically propagates its panic into the joining thread.

cards.statement: A scoped thread's closure can borrow a local `String` that outlives its `std::thread::scope` call.
cards.explanation: Scoped thread functions complete before scope returns, so their closures can borrow local data that outlives the scope.

cards.statement: Cloning an `mpsc::Sender<i32>` gives another producer access to the same channel.
cards.explanation: A Sender clone targets the original channel. Different threads can own these sender handles and send messages to the channel's receiver.

cards.statement: `sync_channel(0)` lets `send` return while its message waits in a buffer for a receiver.
cards.explanation: A zero-bound synchronous channel is a rendezvous channel. Its send waits for a matching receive instead of storing a pending message in a buffer.
cards.misconception: A zero channel bound means messages wait in an unbounded queue.

cards.statement: An `mpsc::Receiver` discards its queued messages when the final sender is dropped.
cards.explanation: Receiver::recv still returns messages queued before disconnection. Once those messages are drained and every sender is gone, it returns Err.
cards.misconception: Dropping the last sender makes buffered messages unavailable to the receiver.

cards.statement: Dropping a `MutexGuard` releases the lock that the guard holds.
cards.explanation: MutexGuard owns the active lock. Its cleanup releases that lock so another thread can acquire it.

cards.statement: A `PoisonError` from `Mutex::lock` contains the acquired guard, retrievable with `into_inner`.
cards.explanation: Mutex poisoning is advisory. PoisonError::into_inner returns the guard so code can inspect or repair the protected data.

cards.statement: Rust's borrow checker rejects a safe program when its mutex lock ordering leads to deadlock.
cards.explanation: Safe Rust programs can deadlock. Two threads that acquire mutexes in opposing orders can wait on each other's locks indefinitely.
cards.misconception: Compile-time borrowing checks prove that safe mutex use is free of deadlocks.

cards.statement: A type `T` implements `Sync` exactly when the reference type `&mut T` implements `Send`.
cards.explanation: Sync corresponds to &T being Send. The relevant reference is shared, because Sync governs safe sharing of a value across threads.
cards.misconception: Sync is defined by sending a mutable reference rather than a shared reference.

cards.statement: Manual `Send` and `Sync` implementations each use a safe `impl` block.
cards.explanation: Manual Send and Sync implementations require unsafe impl. The implementer takes responsibility for upholding the traits' concurrency guarantees.
cards.misconception: The automatically implemented concurrency traits also permit ordinary safe manual implementations.

source.title: Extensible Concurrency with Send and Sync

cards.statement: A Cargo package holds at most one library crate alongside any number of binary crates.
cards.explanation: A package may define multiple executable crate roots, but its library code belongs to a single library crate.

source.title: Packages and Crates - The Rust Programming Language

cards.statement: For crate-root `mod garden;`, Rust can combine definitions from `src/garden.rs` and `src/garden/mod.rs`.
cards.explanation: Rust accepts either module-file location for garden. Providing both locations for that module produces a compiler error rather than combining their contents.
cards.misconception: The compiler merges a module's definitions from both supported file layouts.

cards.statement: Marking a struct `pub` makes its fields part of the struct's public API.
cards.explanation: pub makes the struct type public while its fields retain their own visibility. Mark a field pub to expose that field through the public API.
cards.misconception: Public visibility on a struct propagates to its fields.

source.title: Paths for Referring to an Item in the Module Tree - The Rust Programming Language

cards.statement: Crate-root `pub use inner::Item;` lets callers name a public `Item` as `crate_name::Item`.
cards.explanation: A crate-root pub use exposes the imported name as part of the crate's public API. Callers use the re-exported path even when the original containing module is private.

source.title: Bringing Paths Into Scope with the use Keyword

cards.statement: Cargo interprets dependency version `"0.2.3"` as an exact version pin.
cards.explanation: Cargo treats "0.2.3" as a caret requirement, accepting compatible versions >=0.2.3 and <0.3.0. An exact version requirement has a leading =.
cards.misconception: A complete dependency version string fixes Cargo to exactly that release.

cards.statement: Cargo combines feature requests for a shared normal dependency within the same target build.
cards.explanation: For the same normal dependency version in one target build, Cargo enables the union of features requested by its dependents.

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, a dependency's `resolver = "3"` controls resolution within that dependency's subtree.
cards.explanation: Cargo honors the resolver choice at a workspace's top-level package and ignores dependency settings. A top-level package using edition 2024 defaults to resolver = "3".
cards.misconception: Each dependency's manifest controls a separate resolver for its own dependency subtree.

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, the prelude brings `Future` and `IntoFuture` into scope.
cards.explanation: Rust 2024's standard prelude includes Future and IntoFuture. The compiler makes those traits available through the prelude in ordinary module code.

source.title: Changes to the prelude - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, `fn gen() {}` defines a function named `gen` using an ordinary identifier.
cards.explanation: Edition 2024 reserves gen as a keyword. Use the raw identifier r#gen when a function or variable has that spelling.
cards.misconception: gen remains an ordinary identifier for functions and variables in edition 2024.

source.title: gen keyword - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, Rust keeps an `if let` scrutinee's temporary guard alive through its `else` block.
cards.explanation: In edition 2024, Rust drops temporary guards created while evaluating an if let scrutinee before entering else. Their cleanup happens before that branch runs.
cards.misconception: An if let scrutinee's temporary guard remains alive until the entire conditional finishes.

source.title: if let temporary scope - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, Rust compiles the block `{ let c = std::cell::RefCell::new("x"); c.borrow().len() }`.
cards.explanation: For this RefCell tail expression, Rust drops the temporary borrow guard before the local c. The guard's shorter scope allows c.borrow().len() to compile.

cards.statement: `let p = &raw const x;` creates a raw pointer in safe code when `x` is a local `i32`.
cards.explanation: Creating a raw pointer to a local value is a safe operation. The raw borrow operator produces a pointer rather than accessing memory through that pointer.

source.title: Unsafe Rust - The Rust Programming Language

cards.statement: Rust suspends the borrow checker's reference checks while compiling statements inside an `unsafe` block.
cards.explanation: Rust still checks references inside unsafe blocks. The unsafe keyword enables additional operations while leaving ordinary borrowing rules enforced.
cards.misconception: An unsafe block disables borrowing checks for references.

source.title: Unsafe Rust - The Rust Programming Language

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, Rust warns about raw-pointer dereferences inside an `unsafe fn` outside an `unsafe` block.
cards.explanation: The unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn lint warns by default in edition 2024. An unsafe function declaration does not replace explicit unsafe blocks around its unsafe operations.

cards.statement: Rust accepts a plain `extern "C"` block for foreign declarations in the 2024 edition.
cards.explanation: Edition 2024 requires the block declaration to begin with unsafe extern. Its author takes responsibility for checking the foreign declarations.
cards.misconception: Foreign declaration blocks keep the unmarked extern syntax in edition 2024.

source.title: Unsafe extern blocks - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, `static_mut_refs` denies shared references to `static mut` inside unsafe blocks by default.
cards.explanation: Edition 2024 sets static_mut_refs to deny by default, including references created inside unsafe blocks. This is a lint default rather than an unconditional language prohibition.

cards.statement: Safe code in a 2024 edition crate may call `std::env::set_var` to change an environment variable.
cards.explanation: Edition 2024 marks std::env::set_var as unsafe. Calling it requires an unsafe context and upholding its documented safety conditions.
cards.misconception: Changing an environment variable remains a safe standard library call in edition 2024.

source.title: Unsafe functions - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: Calling an `async fn` starts running its body before it returns the resulting future.
cards.explanation: Calling an async function creates its future and leaves the body unexecuted. Polling that future drives execution of the body.
cards.misconception: An async function begins executing its body as soon as the caller invokes it.

cards.statement: Rust's standard library includes an async runtime that executes a future created by an `async fn`.
cards.explanation: Rust does not bundle an async runtime in its standard library. Runtime crates supply execution machinery that drives asynchronous work.
cards.misconception: The standard library includes the runtime needed to execute async Rust.

cards.statement: The `Future::poll` return type wraps the future's `Output` in `Poll`, including a pending state.
cards.explanation: Future::poll returns Poll<Self::Output>. Poll::Ready carries the completed result, while Poll::Pending carries no output value.

cards.statement: An async closure can be stored behind `&dyn AsyncFn() -> i32` for dynamic dispatch.
cards.explanation: AsyncFn is not dyn compatible. Rust rejects using dyn AsyncFn to erase the concrete callable type for dynamic dispatch.
cards.misconception: The AsyncFn family supports trait objects for async callable values.
